before: IDisposable is an interface for an explicit Dispose operation. It is commonly used for resources such as files; it is separate from the runtime eventually reclaiming object memory.

using (Ticket ticket = new Ticket()) owns the object for that block. Unlike a using System; namespace directive, this form arranges resource cleanup. C# calls Dispose when execution leaves the block, including normal exception unwinding. You do not call it a second time here.

The block prints Working before disposal. Dispose then prints Released in this demonstration; later statements run after that cleanup. Real disposal should release a resource rather than merely printing.

using Ticket ticket = new Ticket(); is another form: cleanup occurs at the end of the enclosing scope, not immediately after that declaration. Do not use a resource after its owning using scope has disposed it.
Expected behavior from this example: Working then Released then After. This expected result is a reasoned prediction until a compiler test is recorded.

Optional local transfer task: Put an inner using block inside an outer one with different cleanup messages; predict the cleanup order. Use a .NET 10 console project with C# 14; reading completion does not verify this local work.
after: A resource is something a program uses, such as an open file. Releasing it may need a clear cleanup step, separate from freeing object memory later.
IDisposable is an interface that requires a Dispose method. Real Dispose methods release resources. This example prints a message so you can see when cleanup happens.
A using block arranges a call to Dispose when the block is left, including when an exception leaves it normally. This is different from a using line that makes a namespace's names available.
The statements inside the block run while the resource is available. Cleanup follows when the program leaves the block.
The program prints Working, then Released, then After. Dispose runs between the inside work and the statement after the block.
A using declaration without a block cleans up at the end of its enclosing scope, the surrounding region of code. Do not keep using a resource after its cleanup has run.
